segments.text: Turn these two phase controls. The light at the pupil stays equally bright, but the focal pattern moves and spreads.
The aperture and total power have not changed.
Which control should we change to make this pattern match the target?
Predict the image forwards, then carry its error backwards to the design.
Here is our one-dimensional pupil, the illuminated opening. We change only its phase, keeping the amplitude fixed.
The phase contains a linear term for tilt and a quadratic term for defocus. Both coefficients are measured in radians.
Watch a phase ramp move the focal pattern sideways.
Add quadratic phase at the same detector plane, and the pattern broadens. Interference redistributes the light.
Multiply the fixed amplitude by a complex phase factor, rotating the field without changing its magnitude. A unitary Fourier transform propagates it while preserving total sampled power.
The detector reads squared field magnitude. Across the full detector grid, these normalized intensities add to one.
Choose the focused pattern with zero tilt and defocus as our target. Start with tilt and defocus coefficients of one point five and two.
Subtract the target intensity at every detector sample. These differences are the residuals, including the pattern's faint outer structure.
Square and sum the residuals, then divide by twice the target's squared norm. This dimensionless loss measures the mismatch.
Keep that target and normalization fixed. Zero loss means matching this sampled intensity, not necessarily recovering a unique phase.
Now ask how a tiny parameter change affects the loss. Follow the same calculation backwards using the chain rule.
A positive residual marks a sample that is too bright. A negative residual marks one that is too dim.
Divide each residual by the target's squared norm, and multiply by the focal field. This starts the reverse intensity calculation.
Apply the conjugate transpose of the Fourier transform. This gathers every detector sample's influence back at the pupil.
This backward field represents mathematical sensitivity. No physical light travels backwards in this calculation.
At the pupil, a small phase change rotates the complex field. That converts field sensitivity into real phase sensitivity.
Weight this sensitivity by position for tilt, and squared position for defocus. Sum across the pupil to obtain both derivatives, the components of our design gradient.
Check those derivatives before using them. Nudge one coefficient forwards and backwards by the same small amount.
Recompute both losses and divide their difference by the separation. This central finite difference estimates the same local slope.
Try several perturbation sizes. Large nudges miss the local slope; extremely small ones expose floating-point rounding.
Here both parameter derivatives agree over a useful range. They are evaluated at the identical starting design.
That checks the implemented derivative. It does not establish that the optical model captures a real device.
Move opposite the gradient to seek a lower loss. The step length controls how far we move.
Surprisingly, the first step increases defocus while reducing the loss. The coefficients act together; shrinking each one is not the rule.
Recompute the loss after each trial. Shorten an unsuccessful step, and accept it only when the loss decreases.
Watch forty updates bring this pattern close to the target, with the same aperture and power throughout.
Start both coefficients at three instead. The loss stalls above zero, although we know a zero-loss design exists.
A correct gradient gives local information, not a guarantee of the best design.
Differentiable optics means an optical model has usable derivatives with respect to its chosen design variables.
Automatic differentiation applies derivative rules through a computation graph. Here, we wrote the reverse calculation explicitly.
Adjoint methods efficiently carry a scalar objective's sensitivity backwards. An automatic-differentiation system can include an optical solver's adjoint.
For curved lenses, the chain must include ray intersections and Snell refraction. Away from grazing incidence, local derivatives follow one intersection branch.
Clipping or switching ray paths can break a smooth local derivative.
For joint optical and digital design, place the loss after reconstruction. Differentiate through both stages to update both sets of parameters.
These are extensions of the chain. Our computed example optimizes only a phase element's intensity pattern.
Predict fields and measurements forwards. Carry a precisely defined loss backwards to the parameters you can change.
Check the derivative, take a step, and measure the loss again.
This model uses one wavelength and ignores polarization. Test what it omits: sensor noise, fabrication limits, and performance beyond the optimized samples.
Differentiable optics connects image error to design changes. A useful gradient still needs a useful model.
